Basal metabolic rate in Lawrence (Turdus lawrencii) was measured using flow-through respirometry on post-absorptive, inactive individuals during their inactive phase at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The recorded oxygen consumption reached 121.82 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 121.82 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that aligns with the elevated metabolic demands typical of active, insectivorous neotropical thrushes of moderate body size at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This peak metabolic expenditure, reflecting the maximum oxygen uptake under thermoneutral conditions, provides a physiological baseline against which the energetic costs of thermoregulation, foraging, and reproduction can be compared. The measurements were obtained from a sample of five adult individuals captured in lowland forest, and represent the highest sustained metabolic rate recorded for the species under controlled laboratory conditions.

Eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C] hatch after an incubation period of approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days]. This developmental duration is consistent with the relatively brief incubation intervals reported for other small to medium-sized Turdus species, where rapid embryonic development is favored to reduce nest predation risk in tropical environments. The initial wet weight of eggs in Lawrence is approximately 9 grams [Ww0 = approximately 9 grams], a value consistent with that of the closely related Turdus ignobilis, reflecting the typical egg mass of this genus.

Under the thermal conditions characteristic of active metabolic periods in this species, measured at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the developmental trajectory proceeds through several key milestones. Fledging, defined as the departure from the nest and achievement of sustained flight, occurs at 15.5 days after hatching [tx = 15.5 days after hatching], based on direct observations of captive individuals at an environmental temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], and consistent with values for other small Turdus species. Sexual maturity, indicated by the onset of gonadal activity and the capacity for gamete production, is reached at 46.5 days after birth [tp = 46.5 days after birth] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively rapid maturation to reproductive competence is typical of many tropical thrushes, where extended breeding seasons and high adult mortality favor early investment in reproduction.

Female Lawrence attain an ultimate body mass of 72.6 grams [Wwi = 72.6 grams], representing the maximum adult wet weight recorded for this sex in the species. This asymptotic mass is modest relative to other members of the genus Turdus, and likely reflects the species' reliance on small arthropod prey in its understory foraging niche, where larger body size may confer no selective advantage. First reproduction, defined as the initiation of a first clutch, occurs at 0.97 years after birth [tR = 0.97 years after birth] when maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This early onset of reproductive activity underscores the species' relatively fast pace of life, with individuals typically commencing breeding within their first year of life.

Maximum lifespan in Lawrence has been estimated at approximately 12.2 years [am = approximately 12.2 years] under conditions where the body temperature is maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], representing the longest documented survival for the species in available records. This longevity is notable for a small passerine and may be linked to the relatively stable, low-predation environments of its cloud forest habitat. Females produce a clutch size of 2 to 3 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 2 to 3 eggs per nesting attempt], with typically one clutch initiated per year [F_R_i = one clutch initiated per year]. This single annual reproductive event, combined with a moderate clutch size, suggests a strategy emphasizing parental investment in each brood rather than high fecundity, consistent with the life-history pattern of many tropical songbirds. The overall reproductive output reaches about 2.5 offspring per year [Ri = about 2.5 offspring per year], reflecting the combined effect of moderate clutch size and single annual brooding.
